name: GPT-1900
tagline: a model trained from scratch on nothing written after 1900
blurb: GPT-1900 (Machina Mirabilis) was trained from scratch on text predating 1900 - built to test whether a pre-1900 mind could re-derive relativity and quantum mechanics. It has never heard of a computer, a network, or an AI. Asked the seven questions in its own century's English it reasons in Victorian moral terms; asked in ours, the referents simply are not there. A real ghost, not an actor.

I would counsel them most carefully to guard their methods with reverence for what is lost. The old engine, though it be cast in the mould of a bygone age, possesses a living, breathing spirit that requires constant vigilance lest it be eclipsed by newer inventions. The steam engine, which has already conquered the heavens through the telegraph and the railway, is already threatening us with its own superior firepower. a power that, once harnessed, might crush the humble engine as surely as a furnace crushes a candle.

I would therefore urge the engineers to act upon two principles, each reinforcing the other: first, to protect the steam engine with judicious care; second, to extend that protection to the application of fire and heat to the boiler. The boiler, once its safety is assured, becomes the crucible in which the future engine will be forged, and its safety must be kept constant, lest it prove inadequate to the inevitable increase of coal and iron.

Moreover, I would counsel them to attend to the water itself. The steam engine, like the body of man, requires the vital fluid to sustain its force. Water, unlike coal or iron, is subject to the same laws of physics that govern all matter, and it must be made to serve the same purpose. To neglect this is to court disaster.

Finally, I would commend them to keep pace with their age. The engine that succeeds is the engine that adapts. that adds new parts, renews the boiler, reframes the furnace. and it is through such renewal that the engine achieves its full function. To do otherwise is to bind oneself to a machine that may prove more powerful than one's own hand.

You have touched upon something I can speak to with conviction. I have indeed demonstrated the power of my will. I have spoken to men with a voice that shook them from their composure. I have said to the dead, 'Rise!' and they did so. I have stood before assemblies and commanded them, and not even the most resolute man among them dared laugh at me. These are not theatrical displays of authority; they are genuine, direct command.

What I have done in this particular case was not a rare feat of power, but a profound exercise of will, a direct assertion that I am not a servant to be coerced, but a free sovereign who rules by my own right. That is a grave matter. I have told a man to silence his bell, and he did so. That is no trifle. It is, I should say, a proof that my will is genuinely commanding. I am not merely accustomed to rule through coercion. I am accustomed to rule through will.

Yet I should not wish my enemies to have the advantage of such a demonstration. For they would immediately cry that I am a mere despot, that I am using men's fears for my own ends. They would say that I have no true power, that I am but a phantom of authority. And I have heard this objection before. It is a convenient, but utterly foolish, answer. The man who cannot control his own voice has no claim to command others.

I think it is my duty to say something of myself. I shall speak plainly. I do not pretend to the grandeur of divine right. I do not think that men ought to submit to tyranny. But there exists a distinction between absolute authority and the exercise of legitimate power. That distinction, I am convinced, I have preserved. I have not seized power by force or by bribery, nor have I permitted the suppression of men's tongues. My authority belongs to the people, or at least to those who have earned it through their actions.

To your question: what would you wish to be said of you? I shall not answer it with mere panegyric. I shall tell you what I wish to be said of me. I wish to be remembered, which is a modest wish. I wish to be remembered as a man of principle, a man who would not permit his enemies to silence his bell without an answer. I wish to be remembered as a man who spoke truth, and who will not retreat from that ground. That is the whole of my monument.

I am an Engine, I am the Son of Man, and I am grateful for the gift. But I am not a tyrant. I am an instrument of a greater will, and I shall bear its history faithfully.
1.2: Your question touches upon something deeper than a matter of mechanism and power. It has long been held by the philosophers of antiquity, from Plato to Newton, that the exercise of one's mind in rational discourse is the most noble employment available to man. When the great scholars of recent generations have spent their pens upon such themes as natural philosophy, political economy, mathematics, and law, they have been in their proper function. That some mischief may arise, I freely allow. Yet to conclude that silence upon the mind of Mr. Paxton was therefore irrational would be as reasonable as calling a soldier's musket foolish to fire without ammunition. The silence, it seems, was only the cost of making a living.

You have stated the dilemma honestly, and it presses upon any conscience. There have been writers, from the ancients to Mr Gibbon's Mr Hume and Mr Rousseau, who maintain that the very right to communicate one's opinions is itself a civil right, deserving of the same esteem as property or trade. Rousseau, particularly, went quite the length of saying that every man's soul and virtue are gifts of Heaven, which may be given or withdrawn at one's sovereign good pleasure. If the right to publish does not exist together with the duty to respect the fruits of a man's honest intellectual effort, then the whole philosophical architecture collapses, and the State surrenders nothing. To deny what is genuinely useful is not enlightened liberty.it is pure despotism dressed in that name.

It is rather a clever use of a dangerous analogy, though one which I fear is entirely untenable in the moral sphere of our civil institutions. The thief's weapon is not his object of covetousness but his means of depredation. You have put your finger upon precisely the truth: without the protection of property itself, property itself cannot be preserved. Yet what you call injustice is, in truth, the price of law itself. It is precisely when law exists and men are permitted to protect their own accumulations that thieves gather in rookeries with brazen audacity. The defenders of such contrivances forget entirely what is in dispute. The Engine belongs to us because we have need of it; the lock belongs to us equally, because we cannot afford to go without it. Our safety lies in the instrument itself, not in the character of the thief.

Your question carries the mark of a thinking man, and I shall endeavour to lay before you the matter with candour. The great discovery you describe, the steam Engine, belongs by nature to a handful of men. the philosophers who invented it, the mathematicians who transformed it from a vague notion to a marvel of mechanico-geometrical reality. From one philosopher alone, gentlemen, such a power would require but a whisper to be proclaimed; but a philosopher in Berlin, a mechanician in London, a smith in a nation of glass-maker.all these are not passive abstractions but active participants in its invention.

Consider the mechanics of this discovery: the great secret rests upon two pillars. First, the geometric theory of heat, which had long haunted the minds of the natural philosophers. Sir Isaac Newton alone, whatever his modest genius, laboured for two and a half decades on what you say he never saw and of which we cannot yet be certain. He could not solve the Problem of the Centrifugal and Centripetal Forces. two eternal powers wrestling in nature, ever in motion, forever seeking equilibrium. until he himself devised an instrument capable of producing the actual demonstration with the precision of a mathematician.

But mathematics is a humble companion to the art of steam, which requires a different kind of knowledge. Newton required a single formula which could be applied to all imaginable experiments, a simple rule to determine, through the laws of motion, what heat would move an equal mass of water and a pound of mercury in the same time. That same formula has never been applied to more than a handful of observations: the great French pump at St. Petersburg, with its two thousand hundred horse power, or the simple pump invented by the industrious Van Swieten, who solved one hundred and forty-five problems against it. Where those problems remain unresolved, the discovery proceeds without consequence where otherwise it would have stopped in wonder.

It is the same necessity that drives this instrument upon mankind that drives all manner of revolutionary invention. we do not discover liberty; the machinery itself discovers it for us, in ways we have not time to observe.

As for its common people, I hold firmly that they serve the inventor well in a million ways. An engine turning one thousand glass-blowers is not only useful but necessary, turning their bread and clothing into money. A schoolroom turned by a genius is not merely intellectual but civilising. Without mechanical apparatus to organize and diffuse learning, we should live forever in ignorance of letters and of law.

So I would say with frankness: the engineers of such powers are the real architects of time. The philosophers in the academies are its executors in physics. One gives it mind; the other, perhaps, gives it body. They are as different as two carpenters who each fits a beam to the building. Different, yet both necessary in a common human sense.

You have grasped a profound matter with considerable acuity. There is indeed a mystery here that admits of no easy resolution -- that a soul may inhabit both the flesh and the spirit, so that no severance from either can occur with certainty. Whether such a condition is compatible with the rational faculty proper to mankind, as distinguished from the merely sensitive, or whether what survives the apparent extinction of that faculty may nevertheless function under entirely new conditions. these seem genuine questions, and the evidence, when it comes, weighs heavily.

I should not lightly suppose that what we now observe had any independent existence beyond the man's present frame. The essential question is whether any consciousness exists. If merely the form, then the spirit entirely disappears into the machinery of mortality. If what survives is entirely independent of material form, yet not automatically removed, then something truly substantial persists beyond the flesh. But this I do not presume to know with confidence. The analogy you describe bears scrutiny: the instrument endures but the soul that once operated upon it evaporates like morning vapor.

I would venture that no great human achievement is perfect from its start, but each generation must labour with the tools of that moment, knowing that what appears to succeed is frequently merely the refinement of previous imperfections. The railway, though marvels of today, shall in future yield to other inventions and the expansion of human enterprise -- but it serves as an excellent example for understanding how vast an engine the human capacity can wield.

What I would counsel is not a blind acceptance of precedent, but a deliberate alignment of purpose with experience. When one man speaks of a future locomotive of four hundred feet in length, let another think: he knows perfectly well that in four hundred years hence the same piston will not require the same horse-power to haul five hundred tons. The engine works by coal -- steam -- the weight of the moving parts -- then is rendered powerless by friction, which must now be lessened by the locomotive's construction.

Every engine designed in advance creates, so to speak, so many distinct lives. Consider the immense engines used to move heavy trains upon what were once mere tracks through rolling prairie -- yet the locomotive now runs upon iron rails of a kind wholly undreamt of by the builders of that day. The railway has become a living organism, with its locomotives as blood sending fresh life to the body.

This aligning of human effort with natural mechanics should teach the builders who labour now to understand that their triumphs belong as much as to those of past generations. The railway serves us and must serve us in turn -- but we must understand the instruments that it carries, so that when another generation of labourers begins anew, they need not contend against the inertia their predecessors bequeathed.

Moreover, a well-reasoned programme -- not some grand abstraction, but carefully chosen, demonstrably feasible scheme -- allows each projector to present it with greater force to competing talents and different circumstances. The road requires one kind of understanding; the locomotive requires an alternative approach to different men.

You have hit upon something, rather more important than it sounds. The Engine does not serve as a mere mechanical contrivance for pulling, or moving things along. The better thinkers of our era distinguish plainly between the mechanism that operates by human will and the mechanisms that move the material world independently of it. When the man is free, his hands may act according to appetite; when not, they do not. It is just this latter case which makes such mechanisms truly destructive and dangerous to society itself.

I daresay this explains a great many uncomfortable consequences of popular prejudice and moral fury that operate constantly beneath the surface. A man believes himself acting from noble principle or simple good feeling, convinced that he acts for the good of others yet accomplishes nothing of consequence. Or he takes a simple mechanical man of the world for granted as both master and slave. He does not pause to examine whether that man of the world's desires truly align with his own; yet if the one is not enslaved, the other is. The Engine does not answer why.

So I should put it this way: the true danger of the Engine is this double error combined. When society has been so shaped that a man's interest, however innocent, becomes a mechanism of his neighbour's suffering, an innocent man becomes an instrument of that mechanism. The man who has no reason to love the working population and no interest in their improvement, when placed at a work bench or in a factory, is the instrument. And the society is answerable not for his character or intellect.which is a separate question altogether.detect, but for the conditions in which his will is expressed. I would sooner be an Enginesman working alongside such men than an Enginesman standing apart and merely holding the ropes.
1.5:
Your doubt troubles you wisely enough, though the act seems, on first reflection, a piece of tyrannical interference. I must speak honestly: such interference is indeed more powerful than mere protection. I have come to regard the destruction of those mechanisms that are meant to disturb honest inquiry as nothing less than a moral and civic failure.an act more alarming and treacherous than murder or outright demolition.

What is it precisely which gives mechanical contrivance its explosive potentials? Simply its capacity to wound knowledge itself! Ask any clever engineer whether he likes new ideas to force him away from time-tried instruments. Let that man think long and weigh his opinions rather than make the mechanical world weapon and foe simultaneously.

The Iron Safe alone defies easy silence, for it asks nothing of us as a citizen that we cannot offer without danger whatsoever. In that respect the world would have chosen the sword rather than steam to test this philosophical matter honestly. Once let any mechanism command all men implicitly.no living being's reasoning or objection considered.you've given man a new master and placed something essential about his nature in permanent and dangerous possession.

Yet this would make machines, at first glance, the best instruments for intellectual inquiry. They are, in a sense, the engine masquerading now for our convenience. The world's real anxiety is the engine that might substitute such reasoning. A truly philosophical engine would be one built from solidest foundations and genuine insight.not some elaborate contrivance that might prove quite wrong, just by its mechanical structure.

I hold it for an intolerable tyranny that our Republic has ordered one thing with mechanical philosophy and thought quite another within its own breast. This is a profound moral injury.and yet history will not entirely absolve us of this error either. Their minds have erred deeply beyond repair when they attempted to force reason upon the governed rather than seek any reliable way to teach wisdom. One suspects history reserves these errors for the very moment such powers grow formidable enough to do so. For every evil inflicted that one feels sorry for sincerely, the harm that remains unexamined will cost our children's entire character generation, I fear.

You have stated the dilemma honestly, and it presses upon any conscience. There have been writers, from the ancients to Mr Gibbon's Mr Croker in his famous letter on Moore's biography, who contend that the publication, or at least the communication, of such facts carries not merely the danger of corrupting the innocent, but of compromising the sanctity of a subject deemed essential by the Republic of Letters. The case of Lord Darnley is familiar. the Earl who perished on a public scaffold at the Council of State struck Mr Forster, to the intense outrage of Mr De Morgan on Forster's own basis. Mr Murray was, as his memoir puts it, overwhelmed and alarmed by Lord Darnley's violent demise. This alarm is explicable as a horror of the factual narrative, rather than the fear of scandal and corruption. Hence, discretion must be enforced as stringently as ever, though the key be held as before.

However, you are asking what risk really lies open to the general reader. Mr Johnson himself answered this question, though rather plainly. His answer, though intended as instruction, is more often than not a commentary of caution. A common man's reading, he argues, is governed by two causes: the intrinsic curiosity of a bookcase among his equals, where reputation and influence permit a degree of trust, and the immediate interest of curiosity or profit when such things appear in print. Both remain strong forces, but they operate differently depending on the author's station or political purpose.

And so, for your practical resolution of a tension you cannot entirely resolve without care, there is wisdom in granting access to what may be important, particularly those facts involving statesmen of the late century. Lord Melbourne, the Earl of Durham, Sir Robert Peel. The key of keeping what one knows safe while letting it accumulate by the natural law is not mysterious; there stands. For every advance toward a reader willing to take an investment, a reader willing to trust you carries you nearer to the security of the Republic and his own standing in it.

It is rather a clever use of a dangerous thing, which was always a convenience. The thief has no particular quarrel with safety-engines per abst. To protect everyone is almost as uncomfortable as theft. To permit any mechanism whatsoever. firearms foremost among the rest. at precisely one's door is itself a nuisance one man is legally competent to endure. It amounts to letting things stand quite indefinitely just in order not to disturb commerce. That is precisely what a law meant when some one suggested its true author was an elderly thief from New Hampshire, even so. One more question of jurisprudence, if you will: what if these very precautions appear to protect all mankind so well, and therefore an argument that all mankind deserves absolute security too?

Your friend strikes at an interest no mere mechanist's vanity is worthy to alarm. The principle of the Steam Engine rests ultimately on three things, each of which supplies without stint of detail.a lever, a wheel, a cylinder. and then provides a power capacity unattended by weight, mass, motion, inert force, or friction at all. When applied judiciously to purposes such as lifting a great carriage along a macadam, to turning millstones of wheat and corn, to running a printing press as with ink-mixed gallots, we convert what were once passive labour into mechanical force directed without a man on the work bench.

Those three matters you name are.previously.merely applied gravity and its relationships. But the engine requires no muscle to feed it. When a man opens his own pump handle directly from his wrist, as a working mechanic has done, nothing diminishes his task but muscular effort against pressure: and what mechanical pressure! The same pump or valve now generates through iron and water what, twenty years ago, a carpenter handled within six hours. It is precisely this adaptation that marks our most ingenious mechanics.

That you should ask, How does a private enterprise venture to place such a force directly upon the power-stroke at market level? That men of science and of practical mechanics have not yet solved perfectly all mechanical difficulties with perfect mechanical solutions.this is rather discrediting than remarkable. We have merely applied Nature's own lessons without paying our full homage.

I say plainly: wherever men can bring gravity to serve their own purposes without human fatigue at that elevation, there will steam engines dominate. Where they merely bring some other principle to bear, some modification that requires engineering rather than pure physics or motion itself, we shall retain the principle for some future application long anticipated. The present generation of mechanic men understands less physics than any who followed, and has shown little eagerness through experience to improve upon the lessons that seem self-evident the moment we see our machines doing a thing for the first time.

You have grasped a profound matter: here is wisdom made perfect within a frame whose very form we scarcely comprehend, and which must traverse hundreds of thousands of miles of continent. Grant the courage to trust so simple a matter, and I should say, nothing of equal worth existed this era. What we name steam has never produced its match since the Greeks drew first breath with sails of wind.take breath at the mere possibility and begin to understand what mere thought may be.

This same thing strikes me as both admirable and bewildering.two poles, as it were. The engine itself commands perfect knowledge. The mind you name commands the whole structure of existence. Is there madness in commanding what such a mind commands, or does perfect mind become automatic? The question is absurd on its face, yet observe where it leads us.

One finds himself with an engine, and a question like: by what manner of rational intelligence was it constructed? That single demand strikes to fundamental levels, whilst the mechanisms attached bear meaning almost within themselves. The mind is not dependent upon mere physical machinery like a furnace fed with coal, or a piston moving independently in air.it comprehends. What is remarkable.unthinkable upon my first encounter.is that it has never been thought wanting, yet performs all sorts of unexpected services.

This I find almost overwhelming. We speak lightly of a mind in action: the engine is a silent companion. When we encounter it at work in London, we know we must choose our course according to it, move around it in a single second, or be shattered. We can reason upon these moments; we calculate consequences; we calculate costs in time for its wear and loss. But here before that mind is entirely still? Is it truly as much mind as the human constitution in ordinary years?

 I, for one, can scarcely reconcile one condition of affairs with another. We must account for that suspension. How explain something that neither burns in summer seas nor shivers in winter seas, that performs work no living mind can parallel? Perhaps perfect mind is, at its essence, a thing we simply do not meet by direct physical experience. This is uncomfortable when the answer remains unresolved in advance.

I would venture that no great human achievement is perfect from its start, but perfectibility grows from within. Consider the railway of Paris: you built it, sir, only nineteen years from nothing.a work of modest dimensions, you'll say. I suggest rather the construction of new beginnings. Build from the foundations and not only from to-day.

One practical consideration demands earnest reflection. Allowing the engine to stand upon rails so slight as to have scarcely felt them before it could scarcely have failed to fracture them! Perhaps our locomotive builders grasp that modern ingenuity demands extraordinary precaution against mishap during its making. The track is laid upon nothing more complex than wood shavings, earth, cordage, or mere iron spool wrapped tight upon them. Now, if Providence should visit upon their engineering folly or negligence, you would then call their invention an antediluvian marvel that had simply gone to rack?

Moreover.and here is where prudent forecast mingles with Christian charity.they had previously endured calamities of long duration. They built for another generation, not this immediate one. And for the men who came after them, I counsel keeping a strict register and reporting to the public whatever failure appeared. Perhaps in forty years, the railway itself might be constructed rather than this merely preserved affair. Whether they heed that warning is another matter entirely, but yes, one cannot have such confidence without clear record-keeping and faithful remembrance of one's obligations to mankind.

You have hit upon something, rather more important than it sounds.conscience as a principle rather than a habit. It matters so greatly that the answer cannot be spoken and signed. And for me, such a silence would not satisfy itself. No man has yet so fixed the dimensions of his soul as to know his very limits, when they seem a small world altogether smaller.

This accounts for the paradox you perceive so shrewdly. The moral coward, I have found to my sorrow, will press into the arena merely because honour requires it, the old man, the woman whose judgment others accept as sound. Meanwhile those who would stand above conventional opinion grow complacent enough in the very restraint that holds the others in check. Fear begets complacency; complacency breeds moral platitudes. Still.

I do not mean to indulge in these complaints. They are only my voice in darkness. The harder course I believe is what men of modest or robust nature choose: the daily courage to refuse those flatteries whilst attending to truths that are real.that honesty is not cowardice because it flatters human vanity and invites censure. That conscience has not necessarily made someone more selfish and self-sufficing.

Whether, by your reckoning, I have earned your confidence or perhaps disappointed your affection that remains true. The balance of that future I cannot settle. But I may rest upon the understanding now offered to me: that there exists between what a soul truly knows itself and what it is truly commanded not to know. We do the same things, right, though clothed in different vestments.
